lessons.title: Recognize Common Plumbing Parts
lessons.objective: Identify common pipes, fittings, and valves
lessons.why_this_matters: Correct product identification begins with understanding what each part does.

lesson_content.heading: Know the basics
lesson_content.text: Pipes carry water or drain waste. Fittings join or change the direction of pipe runs. Valves control flow. Supply lines connect fixtures to water supplies.

lesson_content.heading: Check before recommending
lesson_content.text: Common fitting shapes include elbows, tees, couplings, and adapters. An elbow changes direction. A tee creates a branch. A coupling joins similar ends. An adapter changes connection types.

lesson_content.heading: Put it into practice
lesson_content.text: Names help locate a part, but do not prove that it fits. Size, material, pressure rating, connection type, and use must also match.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer holds a curved fitting and asks for another. Identify it as an elbow, then ask what material and connection style the existing system uses.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Is this for a water supply, drain, or another use? Do you have the old part or its markings?”
common_mistakes: Choosing a fitting by shape alone.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate unclear applications, unusual materials, or safety-critical systems to an experienced specialist.

optional_practice.question: What does a plumbing elbow primarily do?
optional_practice.explanation: An elbow changes the direction of a pipe run.

lessons.title: Understand Pipe Materials and Connections
lessons.why_this_matters: A fitting must suit the pipe material and connection method.

lesson_content.heading: Know the basics
lesson_content.text: Common plumbing materials include copper, PEX, PVC, and CPVC. Their permitted uses and joining methods differ. Do not assume all plastic pipes are interchangeable.

lesson_content.heading: Check before recommending
lesson_content.text: Connections may be threaded, solvent-welded, crimped, clamped, compression, or push-to-connect. Each system has manufacturer instructions, compatible components, and limits.

lesson_content.heading: Put it into practice
lesson_content.text: Identify the material and read the product labeling before making a recommendation. Local code requirements and installation conditions may also apply.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer asks for glue to connect two pieces of plastic pipe. Ask whether the pipe is PVC or CPVC and check the product instructions rather than choosing by bottle color.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Ask: “What material is printed on the pipe, and is this for supply water or drainage?”
common_mistakes: Assuming one cement or fitting works for every plastic pipe.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Ask a qualified plumber or manufacturer support about unmarked pipe, transitions, or code-restricted uses.

choices.A: All pipe materials use the same connection
choices.B: Materials and joining methods have different requirements

optional_practice.explanation: Different pipe systems require compatible fittings and installation methods.

lessons.title: Measure Plumbing Parts Correctly
lessons.objective: Ask for the measurements that matter
lessons.why_this_matters: Nominal pipe sizes and actual dimensions can differ.

lesson_content.heading: Know the basics
lesson_content.text: Plumbing parts may use nominal sizes. The number on the label may not equal a ruler measurement across the outside of the pipe. Different systems use different sizing conventions.

lesson_content.heading: Check before recommending
lesson_content.text: Check the printed size and material markings when possible. Ask for the old fitting or a clear photo showing markings. A measured outside diameter can help identify a system but should not be the only evidence.

lesson_content.heading: Put it into practice
lesson_content.text: Connections also vary by male or female threads and thread style. A size match without the correct connection style can still fail.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer measures a pipe with a tape and requests a fitting. Ask for pipe markings and the connection type before choosing.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Pipe sizes can be named differently from their measured diameter. Let’s confirm the system.”
common_mistakes: Treating a ruler measurement as the product’s nominal size.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate uncertain thread types, mixed materials, and specialty connections.

choices.A: Treat it as the only sizing detail
choices.B: Use it as one clue and confirm markings and system

optional_practice.explanation: Measured diameter helps identification but does not replace system and size verification.

lessons.title: Help With Common Fixture Questions
lessons.objective: Collect useful details before selecting a part
lessons.why_this_matters: A leak symptom may have several possible causes.

lesson_content.heading: Know the basics
lesson_content.text: Customers may ask about faucets, toilets, showerheads, drains, and supply connections. Ask which fixture is involved, where the issue appears, and whether the customer has the model number.

lesson_content.heading: Check before recommending
lesson_content.text: A running toilet might involve more than one component. A dripping faucet may use a specific cartridge. Replacement parts can be model-specific.

lesson_content.heading: Put it into practice
lesson_content.text: Do not promise a repair based on symptoms alone. Help identify a likely product category and verify the manufacturer’s compatibility guidance.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer needs a faucet cartridge. Ask for the faucet brand and model or a photo of the existing cartridge.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Many cartridges look alike. Let’s identify the fixture before selecting one.”
common_mistakes: Promising a universal cartridge will fit.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Refer uncertain repairs, hidden leaks, or water damage to a qualified plumber.

lessons.title: Recognize Plumbing Safety and Escalation
lessons.objective: Identify when a question is beyond retail advice
lessons.why_this_matters: Some plumbing problems risk flooding, contamination, or injury.

lesson_content.heading: Know the basics
lesson_content.text: Active leaks, sewage backups, possible cross-connections, and water-heater issues may require prompt professional attention. Gas lines and gas-fired appliances are not general retail repair topics.

lesson_content.heading: Check before recommending
lesson_content.text: Employees should not advise customers to defeat safety devices or use products outside their listed applications. Potable-water products need appropriate approval for drinking-water contact.

lesson_content.heading: Put it into practice
lesson_content.text: Help customers find information and qualified support. For urgent flooding or immediate hazards, follow emergency and store procedures.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer reports water flowing from a ceiling near a light fixture. Recognize both water and electrical hazards; do not give do-it-yourself instructions.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “That situation may be unsafe. Please seek qualified help promptly rather than trying a part at random.”
common_mistakes: Focusing on selling a fitting while ignoring a serious hazard.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate gas, sewage, water-heater safety, backflow, and combined electrical/water hazards.
